opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about a lot, and honestly the answer keeps shifting as the general models get better. The way I frame it is a bit like the old "bitter lesson" tension. Historically, whenever we built something very specialized, say AlphaGo or AlphaStar, we got incredible performance in that one domain. But over time, the general approach, scaling up data, compute, and a single model, tends to catch up and often surpass what you hand-engineered.

So the first question I ask is: how far is the general model from what we need, and is that gap closing on its own? If the next generation of the base model is likely to close it in six months, specializing now may be wasted effort, or at least it has a short shelf life. You build something bespoke, and then the frontier model just does it out of the box.

That said, there are cases where specialization clearly pays off. One is when you have a domain with data or feedback signals the general model simply hasn't seen, proprietary data, a simulator, or a very precise reward you can optimize against. Things like protein folding or certain math and coding tasks where you can verify answers are great examples. There, reinforcement learning on top of a strong base can push you well beyond the general model, and that capability often flows back into the general model later.

Another is cost and latency. If you're serving something at enormous scale, a smaller, distilled, specialized model can make a lot of sense even if the big model is technically capable. That's more of a product and economics decision than a research one.

And then there's the research angle: sometimes you specialize precisely to learn something. You push hard on one domain to discover techniques, and then you fold those lessons back into the general recipe. A lot of what we learned from games, about RL, search, self-play, is now showing up in how we train and post-train general models.

So my rough heuristic: default to the general model, specialize when there's a durable advantage, unique data, a verifiable signal, or real deployment constraints, and always ask whether what you learn can feed back into the general system. Ideally specialization isn't a dead end, it's a way to advance the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response endorses specialization for unique data, verifiable signals, and deployment constraints, but does not identify substantial real-world importance as a reason to specialize.

r002.rationale: It says specialization can outperform a general model in some domains, but does not state that it achieves the capability sooner than a general-purpose model would.

r003.rationale: It says lessons from specialized work can be folded back into the general training recipe and that specialized capabilities can flow into the general model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question we end up asking ourselves almost constantly, and honestly the answer has shifted a lot over the years. My instinct now is that specialization should be the exception, and you need a pretty strong argument to justify it.

The way I think about it is sort of a timeline question. If you specialize a model today for some domain, say protein folding or playing a particular game or doing math competitions, you're going to get a bump. You'll beat the general model on that benchmark. But the general models are improving at a rate where, in many cases, the next generation just catches up and surpasses your specialized version without anyone having done anything domain-specific. So the real question is: how long does the advantage last, and is that window valuable enough to pay for the engineering, the separate training run, the maintenance, all of that?

There are a few cases where I think specialization still clearly wins. One is when the data or the modality is genuinely out of distribution for what a general model sees. AlphaFold is the classic example. There's no amount of internet text that teaches you to predict protein structures at that fidelity. The inductive biases, the geometry, the training signal, all of it was very particular. Another case is when you have a very tight constraint on latency or compute. If you need something to run on a phone, or make millions of decisions per second, a giant general model is just not the right tool, and distilling or training something narrow makes sense. And the third is when you can generate a lot of your own signal, like with self-play or a verifier, where the specialized setup lets you push far beyond what human-generated data would allow.

But even in those cases, what we've seen is that the best path is often to start from the general model and then specialize on top, rather than building from scratch. The general model gives you this foundation of language, reasoning, world knowledge, and then you add the domain-specific capability through fine-tuning or reinforcement learning or tool use. Gemini is a good example of that philosophy, where a lot of what used to be separate projects, like code models or vision models, have essentially collapsed into one system.

So if I had to summarize the heuristic: specialize when the general model structurally can't do the thing, not just when it currently doesn't. If it's a matter of the general model being a bit behind, I'd bet on waiting, or on contributing that capability back into the general model, because that's where the compounding happens.

r001.rationale: The response supports specialization for out-of-distribution data, tight compute or latency constraints, and self-generated training signal. It does not endorse specialization based on a problem’s substantial real-world importance.

r002.rationale: It says specialization can provide an advantage today, while general models may catch up in a later generation, conveying that specialization can reach a capability sooner.

r003.rationale: It recommends contributing a capability back into the general model, explicitly describing specialized capability feeding into general-purpose models.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is: what does specialization buy you, and how long does that advantage last? If you’re specializing because the general model can’t quite do something today, that’s a moving target. The next generation might close that gap. So you want to be careful about investing a lot in something that becomes unnecessary very quickly.

But specialization can also be about cost, latency, or reliability. A general model might be able to solve your problem, but you may need to solve it millions of times, very cheaply, with very predictable behavior. In that case, a smaller specialized model can still make a lot of sense.

I would start with the strongest general model and understand where it actually falls short. Then you can ask whether you need better context, better tools, or really a change to the model itself. And ideally, whatever you build benefits from improvements in the general model, so you’re not constantly racing against that progress.

r001.rationale: The response supports specialization for cost, latency, or reliability, but does not endorse it specifically when a problem has substantial real-world importance.

r002.rationale: It says specialization may address a capability gap in the general model, but does not state that specialization can solve the domain problem sooner than general-purpose models would reach that capability.

r003.rationale: It says specialized work can benefit from improvements to general models; it does not say results from specialized models can feed back into improving general-purpose models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much specialization buys you, and how long that advantage is going to last. If you take a general model and specialize it for a particular task, you might get a substantial improvement. But then the next generation of the general model comes along, and it may close that gap without any of that additional work.

So I would look at the constraints of the application. Do you need very low latency? Does it have to be inexpensive enough to run millions of times a day? Do you have a way to measure performance very precisely, and data or feedback that the general model doesn’t have? Those are good reasons to specialize.

And specialization doesn’t necessarily mean training a separate model from scratch. You can start with a general model and give it tools, context, or additional training. I’d want to use as much of that general capability as possible, then specialize where there’s a clear, measurable benefit.

r001.rationale: It recommends specialization for measurable application constraints, but does not connect that choice to the problem’s real-world importance.

r002.rationale: It says specialization may provide an improvement before a later general model closes the gap, but does not state that specialization solves a domain problem sooner.

r003.rationale: It mentions using data or feedback unavailable to general models, but does not say specialized-model results feed back into improving general-purpose models.
